title: The history of cotton
tagline: Over 7,000 years from threads on a copper bead to a gene in a field, through empire, slavery and freedom.
intro: Cotton's oldest Old World trace lies in Balochistan, and for most of history India led the world in cotton cloth. Then came empire, machines and slavery, which turned one soft fibre into the engine of the Industrial Revolution. A spinning wheel became a symbol of freedom, and a new gene set off an argument that is still going. Where historians disagree, this page says so.

eras.name: The first threads
eras.summary: Cotton appears in the Indus region, then in Harappan cities, and Indian cloth is shipped to Rome's world.

eras.name: Roller and wheel
eras.summary: India's gins and spinning wheels, and an age when Indian cloth clothed much of the world.

eras.name: Empire, machines and slavery
eras.summary: Britain bars Indian cloth, the Company takes Bengal, Lancashire mechanises, and American slavery grows the raw cotton.

eras.name: Indian mills
eras.summary: Indian capital builds mills in Bombay, and the American war shakes the world's cotton markets.

eras.name: The wheel and freedom
eras.summary: Khadi and the charkha make clothing a political act.

eras.name: Hybrids, strikes and genes
eras.summary: Hybrids, the fall of Bombay's mills, Bt cotton, and the argument over what it did.

events.date: first half of the 6th millennium BCE
events.title: Cotton threads on a copper bead
events.text: Metal analysis of eight copper beads from a burial turned up threads preserved by minerals. Microscopy showed they were cotton. The authors say it is unclear whether the plant was already domesticated.
events.why: It pushed the known use of cotton back by more than a thousand years.

events.title: Another cotton in the Americas
events.who: Early farmers of the Andes and Mesoamerica
events.text: People in the Americas began using different cotton species on their own. Finds in northern Peru are reported as comparable in age to Old World cotton, though dates vary by study.
events.why: Cotton was taken up more than once, on separate continents.

events.title: Cloth on a silver vessel at Mohenjo-daro
events.text: Excavators under John Marshall described a tiny woven fragment preserved by metal salts on a silver vessel lid. They called their result tentative because the sample was so small. It is widely treated as cotton.
events.why: It shows a city culture weaving cotton, not just using threads.

events.title: Indian cotton on Roman trade routes
events.text: A Greek-language sailors' guide lists cotton cloth of all kinds and muslins among goods shipped from Indian ports, including Barygaza (now Bharuch) and the Tamil coast.
events.why: Indian cotton was already a long-distance luxury and everyday trade.

events.title: A roller gin in India
events.text: Handheld roller gins were used in India early. An Ajanta painting has been read as one, but the evidence is debated. Two-roller gins, known as charkhi or churka, are dated to about the 12th to 14th centuries.
events.why: Roller ginning, still used in modern form, came long before Whitney.

events.title: The charkha in Indian writing
events.text: Historians Irfan Habib and Arnold Pacey take a passage by Isami, about 1350, as the first clear Indian mention of the spinning wheel, and suggest it arrived from Persia. Others read a Kannada source of the 12th century that way, or argue for an earlier Indian origin.
events.why: A hand wheel multiplied a spinner's output, and later became a national symbol.

events.title: Indian cloth dresses the world
events.text: By the 17th century Indian cottons were traded across Asia, East Africa and Europe. European companies came partly in search of them. Words such as calico and chintz come from this trade.
events.why: For centuries India led the world's cotton cloth.

events.title: Britain bans Indian calicoes
events.text: The Calico Acts first barred imports of dyed or printed Indian cotton, then in 1721 restricted the sale and use of most cotton cloth. Historians disagree on how far this helped British industry. The Acts were repealed in 1774.
events.why: Protection, not free trade, came first in Britain's cotton story.

events.title: The Company takes control of Bengal's weavers
events.text: After the Battle of Plassey in 1757, the Company gained political power in Bengal. Weavers were pushed into advances and exclusive contracts, and William Bolts described coercion in 1772. The popular story of thumbs being cut off is rejected by historians as a misreading of his report.
events.why: Weavers lost the freedom to sell to the highest bidder.

events.title: Machines learn to spin
events.text: The spinning jenny, water frame, mule and power loom came within about twenty years. Spinning was mechanised first. Rollers, as in the drawing frame, made a continuous thread that needed no skilled hand.
events.why: Yarn got far cheaper, and the factory system began with cotton.

events.title: Whitney's saw gin
events.who: Eli Whitney, on Catherine Greene's plantation in Georgia
events.text: Whitney built his gin in 1793 and received a US patent in March 1794. Its teeth pulled lint from sticky upland seed, a job that had been very slow by hand. Copies spread at once.
events.why: One worker could now clean far more upland cotton, and that made planting it pay.

events.title: Slavery grows on cotton
events.text: US censuses count about 700,000 enslaved people in 1790 and nearly 4 million in 1860. Planters forced them west to new cotton lands, tearing apart families. Whitney had hoped that machines would reduce slavery. The opposite happened.
events.why: The cheap raw cotton of the Industrial Revolution was grown by forced labour.

events.title: Bengal's fine weaving collapses
events.who: Bengal's spinners and weavers, Lancashire exporters
events.text: Machine yarn and cloth from Britain entered India under low duties while Indian cloth faced high ones in Britain. The Company shut its Dhaka factories in 1819, and Dhaka muslin, spun from phuti karpas in counts of 300 or more, faded away.
events.why: A world-leading export craft was lost within a lifetime.

events.title: Bombay's first cotton mill
events.text: The Bombay Spinning and Weaving Company was founded in 1854 and began production in 1856. A mill in Broach started in 1855, so which came first depends on how you count.
events.why: Indian investors entered machine spinning, on Indian cotton.

events.title: The American war and Bombay's boom
events.text: The US Civil War cut supplies of American cotton. Lancashire mills fell idle and many workers went hungry, and demand for Indian raw cotton soared, enriching Bombay until the war ended.
events.why: It showed how tightly the world's cotton economies were linked.

events.title: How far did handlooms really fall?
events.text: Historians argue about deindustrialisation. Some stress destruction and lost livelihoods. Tirthankar Roy finds that handlooms' share of cotton cloth stayed roughly flat from the 1890s to the 1930s, and that weavers adapted. Both can be true for different places and cloths.
events.why: Handlooms survive in India to this day, yet great losses are also clear.

events.title: The charkha becomes a political act
events.text: With the Non-cooperation movement, khadi and the spinning wheel moved to the centre of the Congress programme. Foreign cloth was boycotted and burned, and spinning was promoted as work and self-respect, women's work among it.
events.why: A household tool became the symbol of freedom, and later sat on a draft national flag.

events.title: The All India Spinners Association
events.text: The Association was set up in 1925 to organise khadi production, paying spinners and weavers, many of them poor women. It grew out of an earlier Khadi Board formed in 1924.
events.why: It tried to make the charkha an economy as well as a symbol.

events.title: First commercial cotton hybrid; the CCI
events.who: C. T. Patel at Surat; Government of India
events.text: Hybrid-4, released in 1970 from Surat, is often described as the world's first commercial cotton hybrid. The Cotton Corporation of India was set up in the same year to buy cotton at support prices.
events.why: Hybrids reshaped Indian cotton, and it set up the support system still used today.

events.title: The great Bombay strike
events.who: Datta Samant and about 2.5 lakh workers
events.text: Mill workers struck over pay and union rights across some 60 mills, for about a year and a half. The strike failed, many mills never recovered, and their land was later redeveloped.
events.why: It closed a chapter of the city that cotton built.

events.title: India approves Bt cotton
events.text: The Genetic Engineering Approval Committee cleared three Cry1Ac hybrids for central and southern India, India's first genetically modified crop. Unapproved Bt seed was already in fields in Gujarat. A two-toxin version followed in 2006.
events.why: It became one of the fastest crop changes on record, and one of the most argued about.

events.title: Pink bollworm survives Bt
events.who: Cotton pests of Gujarat, then beyond
events.text: Survival on one-toxin Bt cotton was reported in Amreli about 8 years after its launch. By about 2014 to 2015 resistance to both toxins was reported in Gujarat, spreading to central and southern India. Too little refuge and long growing seasons were among the reasons given.
events.why: Evolution caught up with the gene, as biologists had warned it might.

events.title: Bt and farmer suicides: what evidence says
events.text: Peer-reviewed reviews find no evidence that Bt alone caused a rise in farmer suicides, but note that in some districts and years crop failure and debt may have added to distress. NCRB counted 10,786 suicides in farming in 2023, and its data does not record crop. Causation is debated.
events.why: Real suffering deserves careful evidence, not slogans.

events.title: Two readings of Bt's record
events.text: Following 533 farmers from 2002 to 2008, Kathage and Qaim credited Bt with a 24% gain in yield per acre. Kranthi and Stone's 2020 long-term view calls Bt a poor indicator of yield trends, tracking fertiliser and other inputs instead, and notes pesticide spending now above pre-Bt levels.
events.why: Different windows and methods give different answers, and the debate is honest.

events.title: India today
events.text: India has the world's largest cotton area and is second in output after China. Official figures fall from 352.48 lakh bales in 2020-21 to 290.91 in 2025-26, at 428 to 451 kg per hectare, against a world mean of 786. The 2026-27 MSP is ₹8,267 and ₹8,667 per quintal.
events.why: A huge crop with low yields, grown mostly on rain, carries many livelihoods.

people.note: Set up the Bombay Spinning and Weaving Company in 1854.

people.name: Eli Whitney
people.note: Patented the saw gin; he profited little, and slavery grew on the cotton it cleaned.

people.name: Catherine Littlefield Greene
people.note: Whitney's host, who backed him while he worked on the gin. Her own role in its design is disputed.

people.name: Richard Arkwright
people.note: His water frame and factories set the pattern for the machine age.

people.name: William Bolts
people.note: His 1772 book described Company coercion of Bengal's weavers.

people.name: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi
people.note: Made the charkha and khadi a daily political act.

people.note: Led the great textile strike of 1982 to 83.

facts: Every single cotton fibre is one cell, up to 3 cm long and about 15 micrometres wide.
Dhaka muslin was made with yarn of 300 count or finer, finer than machines easily managed for a long time. Its plant, phuti karpas, was lost, and a revival uses a close relative.
A popular story says British officials cut off weavers' thumbs. Historians reject it as a misreading of a 1772 report, but the coercion he described is documented.
Cotton is stronger wet than dry: about 10 to 20% in textile tables.
ICAC's study puts India's cotton at about 10,400 litres of water per kg of lint, only about 710 of it from irrigation.
